question: What does FAIL mean in fly fishing?
answer: FAIL is an acronym for First Attempt In Learning — the philosophy that failure on the water is not a setback but a prerequisite for improvement. The more you fail, the closer success becomes. Every missed strike, every refusal, every poor cast is data — the raw material of a better angler. The best fly fishers and casting instructors are defined by their willingness to fail publicly, ask questions freely, and remain students of the sport regardless of their credentials.

question: Who was Jim Green and why did he matter to fly fishing?
answer: Jim Green — born in 1920 — was one of the most important figures in modern fly fishing. He started the graphite rod revolution at Fenwick, worked for years at the Sunset Line Company, and held the World Champion casting title with numerous casting merits. He was one of Mac Brown's biggest influences as a teenager — writing six-page letters explaining fly casting mechanics in detail, generously sharing 43 years of accumulated knowledge with a young student who simply asked questions. He was a legend not just for what he knew but for how freely he shared it.

question: What did the NCWRC creel study reveal about fly fisher self-assessment?
answer: The 1993 NCWRC creel study on the Upper Nantahala River found that over 40% of anglers surveyed claimed to be advanced intermediates and 35% claimed to be advanced — yet the top 0.003% of anglers caught significantly more fish than the rest. Over three-quarters of fly fishers surveyed thought much more highly of their abilities than their actual results showed. Pride is the most consistent and least acknowledged obstacle to improvement in fly fishing.

question: What is the Daiwl Bach fly pattern and where does it come from?
answer: The Daiwl Bach — Welsh for "little devil" — is a soft hackle wet fly that has been fishing for nearly 400 years in Ireland and Wales. Mac Brown first encountered it as an eight-year-old when a skilled tobacco farmer on Camp Creek in Greene County, Tennessee handed him a handful of Red Tagged Daiwl Bachs. For decades Mac thought the farmer had invented the pattern. It remains one of the most consistently productive wet fly patterns on the delayed harvest sections of Western North Carolina.

question: How do I find a fly fishing mentor in North Carolina?
answer: The fastest path is quality instruction from a certified professional — someone who has made the same journey and can compress decades of water time into a single lesson. Mac Brown Fly Fish in Bryson City, NC offers private casting lessons, guided trips, and the week-long Fly Fishing Guide School — all built on the same philosophy of generosity with knowledge that Jim Green modeled. The best mentors are those who ask nothing in return but genuine effort from their students.
